a.year_basis: founded (Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen began the collection in 1776; the Albertina marks its 250th anniversary in 2026)
a.year_statement: A Vienna press release says the duke founded the institution in 1776, and it describes the collection as one of the most important print collections in the world.
a.address_statement: The official Albertina contact page gives the address as Albertinaplatz 1, 1010 Vienna, Austria, with the main phone line at +43 1 534 83 0.
a.notes: One conflicting year: Wikipedia's infobox lists establishment as 1805, but the results say it carries a citation-needed tag, while 1776 is given consistently by the museum-linked and other sources, so 1776 is used. Other dates in the results are not the founding: collection passed to the Republic in 1919, the Albertina name taken around 1921, museum re-opened in 2003 after a closure. The results say the Albertina also runs Albertina Modern (Karlsplatz) and Albertina Klosterneuburg (a depot); the historic palace at Albertinaplatz 1 is the address on the official contact page, so it is taken as the main public venue. WebSearch returned summarised text, so the pairing of each sentence with a Links URL rests on the Links list and was not confirmed line by line.

b.year_basis: founded (founded as a private collection by Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen; the museum marks 250 years of existence in 2026)
b.year_statement: The Albertina was founded as a private collection in 1776 and became a state museum in 1919.
b.address_statement: The Albertina's official contact page lists the museum at Albertinaplatz 1, 1010 Vienna, with phone +43 1 534 83 0 (albertina.at/en/contact-us).
b.notes: 1776 is the founding of the collection as a private collection, as stated on the museum's own pages; it is not a public opening. Other dates in the results are different events: the collection became property of the Austrian Republic in April 1919, and the building reopened in 2003 after restoration. One search summary said Wikipedia lists the establishment date as 1805 with a 'citation needed' tag; the museum's own pages and other sources use 1776, so 1776 was taken. The institution also has a second site, Albertina Modern, in the Künstlerhaus, but the main venue at Albertinaplatz is clear.

b.year_statement: Glenstone was founded in 2006 in Potomac, Maryland, by Mitchell Rales and his wife, Emily Wei Rales.
b.address_statement: Glenstone's official contact page lists its address as 12100 Glen Road, Potomac, Maryland 20854, with a main phone line of (301) 983-5001.

Other dates are different events and were not used: Rales bought the land in 1986, and the expanded museum with the Pavilions reopened to the public on October 4, 2018 (glenstone.org press page). One Harvard Club page gives the address as 2100 Glen Road, which looks like a typo; the official contact page says 12100.

a.year_basis: opened to the public in the MuseumsQuartier (Wikipedia: founded in 2001 by Rudolf Leopold)
a.year_statement: With the opening of the Leopold Museum in Vienna's MuseumsQuartier in 2001, this exceptional collection was made permanently accessible to the public.
a.address_statement: The Leopold Museum is at Museumsplatz 1, 1070 Vienna, inside the MuseumsQuartier.
a.notes: Year: the results say a private foundation was set up in 1994 to hold the Leopold collection, before the museum existed; 2001 is used because it is both the opening to the public and the year Wikipedia gives for founding. The exact 2001 opening date differs between sources (20 Sept, 21 Sept, and 5 March from a source the summary calls less reliable), but all say 2001. Address: the search results did not return the museum's own contact page; the address comes from third-party directory listings (basis-wien.at, In Your Pocket), so it is lower confidence than the other three. WebSearch returned summarised text, so the sentence-to-URL pairing rests on the Links list and was not confirmed line by line.

b.year_basis: opened to the public (museum opened in its purpose-built building at the MuseumsQuartier in 2001); the Leopold Museum-Privatstiftung was created as a private foundation in 1994
b.year_statement: The museum's own site says it has been presented in a purpose-built museum at the MuseumsQuartier since 2001.
b.address_statement: The address is listed as LEOPOLD MUSEUM, MuseumsQuartier, Museumsplatz 1, 1070 Wien.
b.notes: Two events appear in the results. The collection was established as a private foundation in 1994 (funded by the Austrian government, the National Bank of Austria and the collector), and the museum opened in 2001. Wikipedia's article on Rudolf Leopold says the museum opened in 2001 with Leopold as director for life, and another summary line says 'It was founded in 2001 by art collector Rudolf Leopold.' 2001 was chosen as the first public opening; if the database wants the legal foundation, that is 1994. One travel site gives 5 March 2001, not confirmed by an official source. The year statement is taken from the search summary, which attributes it to the museum's own site; the official URL listed is the only leopoldmuseum.org museum-history page in that result.

a.year_basis: the Centro de Arte Reina Sofia, forerunner of today's museum, first opened its doors to the public (28 May 1986)
a.year_statement: The Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, the forerunner of today's museum, first opened its doors to the public on 28 May 1986, after its official unveiling two days previously.
a.address_statement: The museum is at Calle Santa Isabel, 52, 28012 Madrid, according to its own contact page.
a.notes: Sources give different years for different events, so this is a judgment call. 1986: Centro de Arte Reina Sofia first opened to the public (the museum's 40th anniversary press note, titled 'The Reina Sofia Turns 40', is consistent with this; the month varies between results: April, 28 May, September). 1988: became the national museum by royal decree on 27 May 1988 (a status change, not a first opening). 1990: the museum's own history page says it opened its doors in 1990 as a national museum, and another result gives 31 October 1990 after a reform. 1992: permanent collection inaugurated on 10 September 1992; Wikipedia's infobox lists this as establishment. If the database wants the national museum rather than its forerunner, 1988 or 1990 would apply. The 1986 figure rests on results that call the Centro the forerunner, so it is treated as the same body with a later status change. Address: the contact page found was on the static4.museoreinasofia.es subdomain of the museum's own domain. WebSearch returned summarised text, so the sentence-to-URL pairing rests on the Links list and was not confirmed line by line.

b.year_basis: opened (as the Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, which opened with temporary exhibitions in April 1986; it became the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía by decree in 1988)
b.year_statement: In 1980, restoration work began on the building, under the direction of Antonio Fernández Alba, and in April 1986 the Centro de Arte Reina Sofía opened with temporary exhibitions.
b.address_statement: The official contact page lists the museum at Calle Santa Isabel, 52, 28012 Madrid, with a phone line of (+34) 91 774 1000.
b.notes: The results give several dates for different events, and the museum's own pages are not fully consistent about the public opening. The Centro de Arte Reina Sofía opened in April 1986 (museum history page); an earlier search summary said another source gave September 1986 as the founding, which is also 1986. It became a national museum on 27 May 1988 (museum history page). The permanent collection was inaugurated on 10 September 1992. A search summary said a 2020 museum dossier states the Museo opened its doors to the public on 31 October 1990, and that Wikipedia gives 10 September 1992 as the official inauguration; I could not read those pages. 1986 was chosen as the first opening as a body, under its original name; if the database wants the national-museum or permanent-collection date, it would be 1988 or 1992. The Nouvel Building opened in 2005 and is not the founding. The museum also has other venues in Madrid, but Calle Santa Isabel is its main address.

a.address_statement: The National Gallery of Australia's physical address is Parkes Place, Parkes, Canberra ACT 2600.
a.notes: Year: the results also describe earlier collecting from 1910 and a building that opened in 1982, so 1967 is the year the results call 'established'; the search summary did not tie that sentence to one page, so Wikipedia is cited as the nearest listed source and the gallery's own history page was not retrieved. Address: taken from the gallery's own pages, which give no street number. Postal address is GPO Box 1150, Canberra ACT 2601. b.year_basis: established (by the Australian Government, originally as the Australian National Gallery)
b.year_statement: The National Gallery of Australia (NGA) was established in 1967 by the Australian Government as a national public art museum, and it was originally called the Australian National Gallery.
b.address_statement: The National Gallery of Australia's address is Parkes Place, Canberra ACT 2600, and its general contact details from archived gallery pages are below.
b.notes: Year: the same results say the gallery building opened in 1982 after fourteen years of planning, design and construction. I treated that as the building, not the founding of the body, and kept 1967 (established). 1 Nov 1967 is also when the government announced it would build the building. The text did not make clear which exact URL carries the 1967 sentence; I attributed it to the Wikipedia result. Address: the results do not list a street number. A second search gave 'Parkes Place, Parkes ACT 2600' (suburb Parkes instead of Canberra) with the same postcode, and said the current nga.gov.au/visit page exists, but the displayed text did not show the address from that page. a.year_basis: founded by King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia as the Königliche Museen (Royal Museums)
a.year_statement: King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia founded the museum in 1823 as the Königliche Museen (Royal Museums).
a.notes: Year: 1823 comes from Wikipedia only; the smb.museum history page summaries did not state 1823. If 'first opened to the public' is the wanted event, the results point to 1830 (Altes Museum, opened 3 August 1830), but that is one building, not the body. Address left empty: the institution is a group of museums on many sites (17 museums in five clusters per Wikipedia, 19 per the smb.museum simple-language page, described as 'spread over many different sites'), and no single main public venue is identified.

a.year_basis: opened to the public as a museum, by Grand Duke Peter Leopold (per the Uffizi's own About us page)
a.year_statement: Public museum: Grand Duke Peter Leopold opened it to the public as a museum in 1769 ([About us](https://www.uffizi.it/en/pages/about-us)).
a.address_statement: The official Uffizi Galleries website gives the address as Piazzale degli Uffizi 6, 50122 Florence, Italy, with ticket support available by phone from 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ([uffizi.it contact page](https://www.uffizi.it/en/contacts)).
a.notes: Other results gave different years for different events. The building ran from 1560 to 1580 or 1581 (construction, not used). The gallery was open to visitors by request since the sixteenth century. It formally became a museum in 1865. A Wikipedia revision from 2022 and one other lower-grade source gave 1765 for public opening. The Uffizi's own site and Britannica, as relayed in the results, give 1769, so 1769 is used on the strength of the official site; the 1765 figure is a conflict from weaker sources. The address is the Uffizi Gallery at the Palazzo degli Uffizi; the Uffizi Galleries organisation also runs other venues, which were not examined.

b.address_statement: The official Uffizi Galleries address is Piazzale degli Uffizi 6, 50122 Florence, Italy (Piazzale degli Uffizi 6 50122 Florence, Italy.).
b.notes: Year left at 0: the results give several different events and sources disagree on which one counts as opening. The building was begun in 1560 by Giorgio Vasari for Cosimo I and completed in 1581; one source says the gallery had been open to visitors by request since the sixteenth century, was officially opened to the public in 1769, and formally became a museum in 1865; another says it was open to visitors since the 16th century but only formally became a museum in 1865. The official uffizi.it About us page appeared in the Links (https://www.uffizi.it/en/pages/about-us) but no year from it was shown in the results text, and the history results were third-party sources. Address: the institution is the Gallerie degli Uffizi, which also runs other venues (the results list uffizi.it pages for the Pitti Palace and Palatine Gallery); the address given is the Galleries' official address and registered office, Piazzale degli Uffizi 6, and it is the Uffizi Gallery's own address in other listings.

a.notes: Year left at 0 because the sources disagree and the museum's own site is inconsistent with itself. Results said: 'The Manchester Museum was opened to the public in 1888' (Wikipedia and several sites); the University's history page says the Museum 'was opened in 1887'; a Bridgeman biography says 1890; Wikipedia gives 1867 as the establishment date; the museum's own history page says the collections went to Owens College in 1868, while another page on the same site says 1867. The address result text did not say which of the museum.manchester.ac.uk links carried the sentence, so the Plan your visit page and the home page from that same result list are both given. The collection began with John Leigh Philips; the Manchester Natural History Society was set up in 1821; the collection was displayed on Peter Street from 1835; the collections passed to Owens College in 1868 (per the museum's own site); the museum opened on its present Oxford Road site in a building by Alfred Waterhouse, dated 1887 by the University's history page but 1887 and 1890 by other sources. It cannot be told from the results which of these is the founding of the museum as a body. Address: the official site gives only 'Oxford Road, Manchester M13 9PL' with no street number; a non-official arts directory gave 'The University of Manchester, Oxford Road, Manchester, M13 9PL'. The result text did not name which museum.manchester.ac.uk page carries the address, so the plan-your-visit and maps pages are the likely sources among the links returned.
